'''white-gum''' (hwīt′gum), ''n.'' In ''med.'', an eruption of whitish spots surrounded by a red areola, occurring about the neck and arms of infants; strophulus albidus.

'''white-handed''' (hwīt′han″ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having white hands.
{{smaller block|''White-handed'' mistress, one sweet word with thee.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 230.}}}}
'''2.''' Having pure, unstained hands; not tainted with guilt.
{{smaller block|<poem>O, welcome, pure-eyed Faith; ''white-handed'' Hope,
Thou hovering angel, girt with golden wings!</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 213.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''zoöl.'', having the fore paws white: as, the ''white-handed'' gibbon, ''Hylobates lar''. See cut under ''gibbon''.

'''white-hass''' (hwīt′has), ''n.'' A white-pudding, stuffed with oatmeal and suet. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|There is black-pudding and ''white-hass''—try whilk ye like best.
{{right|''Scott'', Bride of Lammermoor, xii.}}}}

'''whitehause''' (hwīt′hâz), ''n.'' [< ''white'' + ''hause'', var. of ''halse''<sup>1</sup>.] The shagreen ray, ''Raia fullonica'', a batoid fish common in British waters. [Local, Eng.]

'''whitehead''' (hwīt′hed), ''n.'' '''1.''' The white-headed scoter or surf-scoter, a duck, ''Œdemia perspicillata''. See cut under ''Pelionetta''. [Long Island.] —'''2.''' A breed of domestic pigeons with the head and tail white; a white-tailed monk.—
readings.c2s2:
'''3.''' The blue wavey, or blue-winged snow-goose, ''Chen cærulescens.'' See ''goose.''—'''4.''' The broom-bush, ''Parthenium Hysterophorus.'' Also called ''bastard feverfew'' and ''West Indian mugwort.'' [West Indies.]

¶
'''white-headed''' (hwīt′hed″ed), ''a.'' Having the head more or less entirely white: specifying many animals.—{{smaller|'''White-headed duck,''' ''Erismatura leucocephala,'' a rudder-tailed or stiff-tailed duck of Europe and Africa.—'''White-headed eagle,''' the common bald eagle or sea-eagle of North America, ''Haliaëtus leucocephalus.'' See ''eagle.''—'''White-headed goose, gull, shrike.''' See the nouns.—'''White-headed harpy.''' See ''harpy,'' 3 (''b'').—'''White-headed tern,''' ''Sterna trudeaui,'' a South American species of tern.—'''White-headed titmouse,''' a variety of the long-tailed titmouse, ''Acredula caudata'' (or ''rosea''), whose head is whiter than usual. It inhabits northerly continental Europe.—'''White-headed woodpecker,''' ''Picus'' or ''Xenopicus albolarvatus,'' a woodpecker with a black body, white head, scarlet nuchal band in the male, and white wing-patch, found in the forests, chiefly of conifers, of the Pacific slope of the United States. See cut under ''Xenopicus.''}}

'''Whitehead’s operations.''' See ''operation.''

'''white-horse''' (hwīt′hôrs), ''n.'' '''1.''' An extremely tough and sinewy substance resembling blubber, but destitute of oil, which lies between the upper jaw and the junk of a sperm-whale. ''C. M. Scammon,'' Marine Mammals, p. 312.—'''2.''' A West Indian rubiaceous shrub, ''Portlandia grandiflora,'' having whitish flowers 3 to 8 inches long.

'''white-hot''' (hwīt′hot), ''a.'' Heated to full incandescence so as to emit all the rays of the visible spectrum, and hence appear a dazzling white to the eye. See ''radiation'' and ''spectrum,'' and ''red heat, white heat'' (under ''heat'').

'''whiteness''' (hwīt′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''whytnesse'', ''whitnesse''; < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.] '''1.''' The state of being white; white color, or freedom from any darkness or obscurity on the surface.
{{smaller block|Says Al Kittib, they [the Moors] displayed teeth of dazzling ''whiteness'', and their breath was as the perfume of flowers.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, i.}}}}
'''2.''' Lack of color in the face; paleness, as from sickness, terror, or grief; pallor.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou tremblest; and the ''whiteness'' in thy cheek
Is apter than thy tongue to tell thy errand.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 1. 68.}}}}
'''3.''' Purity; cleanness; freedom from stain or blemish.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am she,
And so will bear myself, whose truth and ''whiteness''
Shall ever stand as far from these detections
As you from duty.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, i. 1.}}
<poem>He had kept
The ''whiteness'' of his soul, and thus men o’er him wept.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iii. 57.}}}}

'''whitening''' (hwīt′ning), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''whiten'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The act or process of making white. —'''2.''' In ''leather-manuf.'', the operation of cleaning and preparing the flesh side of a hide on a beam, preparatory to waxing.—'''3.''' Tin-plating. See ''chemical plating'', under ''plate'', ''v. t.''—'''4.''' Same as ''whiting''<sup>1</sup>.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|white-eye|6911|whitening}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|By most English-speaking people in various parts of the world the prevalent species of Zosterops is commonly called “''White-eye''” or “Silver-eye” from the feature before mentioned.
{{right|''A. Newton'', Encyc. Brit., XXIV. 824, note.}}}}

'''white-eyed''' (hwīt′īd), ''a.'' Having white eyes—that is, eyes in which the iris is white or colorless.—{{smaller|'''White-eyed pochard.''' See cut under ''Nyroca.''—'''White-eyed shad.''' Same as ''mud-shad.''—'''White-eyed towhee,''' a variety of the common towhee bunting, found in Florida—''Pipilo erythrophthalmus alleni.'' Compare cut under ''Pipilo.''—'''White-eyed vireo''' or '''greenlet.''' See ''Vireo'' (with cut).—'''White-eyed warbler†.''' See ''warbler.''}}

'''white-faced''' (hwīt′fāst), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having a white or pale face, as from fear or illness.—'''2.''' Having a white front or surface.
{{smaller block|That pale, that ''white-facèd'' shore.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|On a rickety chair, tilted against the ''white-faced'' wall, sat a young man, wearing a suit of exceedingly cheap and shabby store-clothes.
{{right|''The Atlantic'', LXI. 676.}}}}
'''3.''' Marked with white on the front of the head, as a bird or other animal.—{{smaller|'''White-faced black Spanish fowl.''' See ''Spanish fowl'', under ''Spanish.''—'''White-faced duck.''' (''a'') The female scaup-duck, ''Fuligula marila'', which has a white band about the base of the bill. See cut under ''scaup.'' (''b'') The blue-winged teal. See cut under ''teal''<sup>1</sup>.—'''White-faced goose.''' See ''goose.''—'''White-faced hornet.''' See ''Vespa.''—'''White-faced ibis,''' ''Ibis guarauna'', related to the glossy ibis, but having the parts about the bill white: found in western parts of the United States.—'''White-faced type.''' See ''type'', 8.}}

'''white-favored''' (hwīt′fā″vo̤rd), ''a.'' Wearing white favors, as in connection with a wedding.
{{smaller block|<poem>But they must go, the time draws on,
And those ''white-favour’d'' horses wait.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, Conclusion.}}}}

'''Whitefieldian''' (hwit-fēl′di-an), ''n.''   [< ''Whitefield'' (see def.) + ''-ian.'']   A follower of George Whitefield, after his separation from the Wesleys: same as ''Huntingdonian.''

'''whitefish''' (hwīt′fish), ''n.'' A general name of fishes and other aquatic animals which are white, or nearly so: variously applied. {{smaller|(''a'') A fish of such kind as the whiting, haddock, or menhaden. (''b'') Any fish of the genus ''Coregonus.'' These are important food-fishes of both American and European waters, representing a division (''Coregoninæ'') of the family ''Salmonidæ.''}}
{{smaller|Most of the species have their distinctive names, for which see ''Coregoninæ'' and ''Coregonus.'' See also cuts under ''cisco'' and ''shadwaiter.'' (''c'') Any fish of the genus ''Leuciscus.'' (''d'') Any white whale, or beluga. See ''beluga'', 2, and cut under ''Delphinapterus.'' (''e'') Same as ''blanquillo'', 2.}}—'''Whitefish-mullet.''' {{smaller|See ''mullet''<sup>1</sup>.}}

[[File:century v08 p0715 c1f1.png|center|307px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Whitefish of the Great Lakes (''Coregonus clupeiformis'').}}}}

'''whiteflaw†''' (hwīt′flâ), ''n.''   [A var. of ''whickflaw'', simulating ''white''<sup>1</sup>.]   A whitlow.
{{smaller block|A cock is offered (at least was wont to be) to St. Christopher in Touraine for a certaine sore, which useth to be in the end of men’s fingers, the ''white-flaw.''
{{right|''World of Wonders'', p. 308. (Quoted in N. and Q., 7th ser., [X. 511.)}}}}
{{smaller block|The nails faln off by ''Whit-flawes.''
{{right|''Herrick'', Oberon’s Palace.}}}}

'''white-flesher''' (hwīt′flesh″ėr), ''n.'' The ruffed grouse, ''Bonasa umbellus:'' so called in distinction from grouse with dark meat. ''Sir John Richardson'', 1831. [Canada.]

'''white-flowered''' (hwīt′flou″ėrd), ''a.'' Noting numerous plants with white flowers: as, ''white-flowered'' azalea, broom, cinquefoil, etc.

'''white-footed''' (hwīt′fu̇t″ed), ''a.'' Having white feet: as, the ''white-footed'' hapalote, ''Hapalotis albipes'', of New South Wales.—{{smaller|'''White-footed mouse,''' ''Vesperimus americanus'', the commonest vesper-mouse of North America, with snowy paws and under parts—features shared by most of the mice of the genus ''Vesperimus.'' See ''Vesperimus'', and cut under ''deer-mouse.''}}

'''white-fronted''' (hwīt′frun″ted), ''a.'' Having the front or forehead white, as a bird. {{smaller|The white-fronted dove is ''Engyptila albifrons'', found in Texas and Mexico. The white-fronted goose is ''Anser albifrons'' of Europe, a variety of which, ''A. albifrons gambeli'', inhabits North America, and is known in some parts as the ''speckle-belly.'' The white-fronted lemur of Madagascar is a species or variety which has been named ''Lemur albifrons.'' The white-fronted capuchin is ''Cebus albifrons,'' a South American monkey.}}

'''white-grass''' (hwīt′grȧs), ''n.'' See ''Leersia.''

'''white-grub''' (hwīt′grub), ''n.'' The large white earth-inhabiting larva of any one of a number of scarabæid beetles. {{smaller|The common white-grub of Europe is the larva of the cockchafer, ''Melolontha vulgaris;'' that of the more northern United States is the larva of the May-beetle, ''Lachnosterna fusca'', and congeneric dor-bugs; and that of the southern United States is usually the larva of the June-bug, ''Allorhina nitida.'' All feed upon the roots of grass and other vegetation, and at times are serious pests. See ''Allorhina'' (with cut), ''cockchafer'', ''dor-bug'' (with cut), ''June-bug'' (with cut), ''Lachnosterna'', ''May-beetle'', and ''Melolontha''.}}

'''white-gum''' (hwīt′gum), ''n.'' In ''med.'', an eruption of whitish spots surrounded by a red areola, occurring about the neck and arms of infants; strophulus albidus.

'''white-handed''' (hwīt′han″ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Having white hands.
{{smaller block|''White-handed'' mistress, one sweet word with thee.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., v. 2. 230.}}}}
'''2.''' Having pure, unstained hands; not tainted with guilt.
{{smaller block|<poem>O, welcome, pure-eyed Faith; ''white-handed'' Hope,
Thou hovering angel, girt with golden wings!</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 213.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''zoöl.'', having the fore paws white: as, the ''white-handed'' gibbon, ''Hylobates lar''. See cut under ''gibbon''.

The broom-bush, ''Parthenium Hysterophorus.'' Also called ''bastard feverfew'' and ''West Indian mugwort.'' [West Indies.]

See ''eagle.''—'''White-headed goose, gull, shrike.''' See the nouns.—'''White-headed harpy.''' See ''harpy,'' 3 (''b'').—'''White-headed tern,''' ''Sterna trudeaui,'' a South American species of tern.—'''White-headed titmouse,''' a variety of the long-tailed titmouse, ''Acredula caudata'' (or ''rosea''), whose head is whiter than usual. It inhabits northerly continental Europe.—'''White-headed woodpecker,''' ''Picus'' or ''Xenopicus albolarvatus,'' a woodpecker with a black body, white head, scarlet nuchal band in the male, and white wing-patch, found in the forests, chiefly of conifers, of the Pacific slope of the United States. See cut under ''Xenopicus.''}}

M. Scammon,'' Marine Mammals, p. 312.—'''2.''' A West Indian rubiaceous shrub, ''Portlandia grandiflora,'' having whitish flowers 3 to 8 inches long.

'''white-hot''' (hwīt′hot), ''a.'' Heated to full incandescence so as to emit all the rays of the visible spectrum, and hence appear a dazzling white to the eye. See ''radiation'' and ''spectrum,'' and ''red heat, white heat'' (under ''heat''). {{smaller block|''White-hot'' iron we are familiar with, but ''white-hot'' silver is what we do not often look upon.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Emerson, ix.}}}}

'''white-leg''' (hwīt′leg), ''n.'' The disease phlegmasia dolens; milk-leg. See ''phlegmasia.''

'''white-limed''' (hwīt′līmd), ''a.''   [< ME. ''whitlymed;'' < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''limed.'']   Whitewashed.
{{smaller block|Ypocrisie . . . is ylikned in Latyn to a lothliche dounghep,
That were by-snywe al with snow and snakes withynne,
Or to a wal ''whit-lymed'' and were blak with-inne.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xvii. 267.}}}}

'''white-line''' (hwīt′līn), ''a.'' White-lined.—'''White-line dart,''' {{smaller|a British noctuid moth, ''Agrotis tritici.''}}

'''white-lined''' (hwīt′līnd), ''a.'' Having a white line or lines.—'''White-lined morning-sphinx,''' {{smaller|a common North American sphingid moth, ''Deilephila lineata.'' See ''sphinx'' (with cut).}}

'''white-lipped''' (hwīt′lipt), ''a.'' Having white lips; having a white lip or aperture, as a shell. —'''White-lipped peccary,''' {{smaller|''Dicotyles labiatus.''}}—'''White-lipped snail,''' {{smaller|the common garden-snail, girdled snail, or brown snail, ''Helix nemoralis'' (including ''H. hortensis'' and ''H. hybrida''). Also called ''white-mouthed snail.''}}

'''white-listed''' (hwīt′lis″ted), ''a.'' Having white stripes or lists on a darker ground (the tree in the quotation having been torn with lightning).
{{smaller block|<poem>He raised his eyes and saw
The tree that shone ''white-listed'' thro’ the gloom.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Merlin and Vivien.}}}}

'''white-livered''' (hwīt′liv″ėrd), ''a.'' Having (according to an old notion) a light-colored liver, supposed to be due to lack of bile or gall, and hence a pale look—an indication of cowardice; hence, cowardly.

{{smaller block|For Bardolph, he is ''white-livered'' and red-faced; by the means whereof a’ faces it out, but fights not.
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 2. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|As I live, they stay not here, ''white-liver’d'' wretches!
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Elder Brother, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|When they come in swaggering company, and will pocket up anything, may they not properly be said to be ''white-livered?'' {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, iv. 1.}}}}

'''whitely†''' (hwīt′li), ''a.''   [< ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   White; pale.
{{smaller block|A ''whitly'' wanton, with a veluet brow.
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iii. 1. 198 (folio 1623).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Could I those ''whitely'' Stars go nigh
Which make the Milky-Way in Sky.</poem>
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 22 (song).}}}}

'''white-marked''' (hwīt′märkt), ''a.'' Marked with white, as various animals.—'''White-marked moth,''' {{smaller|''Tæniocampa leucographa'', a British noctuid.}}—'''White-marked tussock-moth,''' {{smaller|a common North American vaporer, ''Orgyia leucostigma.'' See ''tussock-moth'', and cut under ''Orgyia'', 2.}}

'''white-meat''' (hwīt′mēt), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whitmete''; < ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''meat''.]   See ''white meat'', under ''white''<sup>1</sup>.

'''white-mouthed''' (hwīt′moutht), ''a.'' In ''conch.'', white-lipped.

'''whiten''' (hwī′tn), ''v.''   [< ME. ''hwitnen'' = Icel. ''hvītna'' = Sw. ''hvitna'' = Dan. ''hvidne'', whiten, become white; as ''white''<sup>1</sup> + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become white; turn white; bleach: as, the sea ''whitens'' with foam.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Whiten'' gan the orisounte sheene
Al esterward, as it is wont to done.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 276.}}}}
{{smaller block|Willows ''whiten'', aspens quiver.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lady of Shalott.}}}}

{{smaller block|Fields like prairies, snow-patched, as far as you could see, with things laid out to ''whiten!''
{{right|''Mrs. Whitney'', Leslie Goldthwaite, vi.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To make white; bleach; blanch; whitewash: as, to ''whiten'' cloth; to ''whiten'' a wall.
{{smaller block|Drooping lilies ''whitened'' all the ground.
{{right|''Addison'', tr. of Virgil’s Georgics, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|It [the mastic] is chewed only by the Turks, especially the ladies, who use it both as an amusement and also to ''whiten'' their teeth and sweeten the breath.
{{right|''Pococke'', Description of the East, II. ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|The walls of Churches and rich Mens Houses are ''whitened'' with Lime, both within and without.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 140.}}}}

{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' ''Whiten, Bleach, Blanch, Etiolate. Whiten'' may be a general word for making white, but is chiefly used for the putting of a white coating upon a surface: as, a wall ''whitened'' by the application of lime; the sea ''whitened'' by the wind. ''White'' for ''whiten'' is old-fashioned or Biblical. ''Bleach'' and ''blanch'' express the act of making white by removal, change, or destruction of color. ''Bleaching'' is done chemically or by exposure to light and air: as, to ''bleach'' linen or bones. ''Blanching'' is a natural process: celery and other plants are ''blanched'' or ''etiolated'' by excluding light from them; cheeks are ''blanched'' by fear, when the blood retires from their capillaries and leaves them pale. See also defs. 5 and 6 under ''blanch''.}}

'''white-necked''' (hwīt′nekt), ''a.'' Having a white neck: specifying various animals: as, the ''white-necked'' raven, ''Corvus cryptoleucus'', a small raven found in western parts of the United States, having the concealed bases of the feathers of the neck fleecy-white; the ''white-necked'' or chaplain crow, ''Corvus scapulatus;'' the ''white-necked'' otary, an Australian eared seal.

'''whitener''' (hwīt′nėr), ''n.''   [< ''whiten'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who or that which bleaches, or makes white; especially, some chemical or other agent used for bleaching or cleaning very perfectly.
